Um, I'm happy every time a Mac gets shipped.
I still have people, you know, sending me emails telling me how much they love their Macs.
Um, and it's sort of, how do you explain it?
It's it's it's like the first uh person you were ever in love with, you know?
It's like your first love and there will never be another one like it.
Um, you know, and in my case, you know, we we uh we were together for 10 years and uh that's a long time.

Yeah.
Until recently with Motorola.
Yeah, you don't know.
Who knows?
Okay.
I have no idea.

I usually believe that if, you know, if if um if one group of people didn't do something, uh within a certain number of years, the times would produce another group of people that would accomplish similar things.
Uh, we happen to be at the right place, exactly the right time with the right group of people and we did some wonderful work.
I I'm extraordinarily proud of the work that the team at Apple did when I was there.
And I think that uh personally our major contribution was was a little different than than some people might think.
Um, I think our major contribution was in bringing a liberal arts point of view to uh the use of computers.

Uh what I mean by that is that, you know, if you really look at the ease of use of the Macintosh, the the driving motivation behind that was to bring uh not only ease of use to people so that many, many more people could use computers for non-traditional things at that time.
Um, but it was to bring, you know, beautiful fonts and typography to people.
It was to bring graphics to people, not for, you know, plotting uh laminar flow calculations, but so that they could see beautiful, you know, photographs or pictures or artwork, uh etc.
Uh to help them communicate what they were doing potentially.
Our our goal was to bring a liberal arts perspective and a liberal arts audience to what had had traditionally been uh, you know, a very geeky technology and a very geeky audience.

Because in my perspective and the way I was raised was that um that that science and and computer science is a liberal art.
It's something that everyone should know how to use at least and harness uh in their life.
It's not something that should be, you know, should be relegated to uh to 5% of the population over in the corner.
It's something that everybody should be exposed to, everybody should should have a mastery of to some extent.
And um that's how we viewed, you know, computation or these computation devices.

Um, eventually.
You know, it's in the pro it's Apple certainly, that that's the seed of Apple.
Um, you know, computers for the rest of us.
And I I think the the sort of uh the liberal arts point of view still lives at Apple.
I'm not so sure that it lives that many other places.
Mhm.
I mean, one of the reasons I think Microsoft took 10 years to copy the Mac was because they didn't really get it at its core.

That's a really big question.
Um, I think the PC as we know it's going to be around for quite some time, but but the the the heart of the question is, are we entering a time window where we might see the first successful post PC devices.

Well, you know, I don't know what a corporate lifestyle is.
I mean Apple was a was a corporation.
We were very conscious of that.
We were very driven to make money so that we can continue to invest in the things we loved.
Uh I I would say Apple was a corporate lifestyle, but it had a few very big differences to other corporate lifestyles that I'd seen.
The first one was uh a real belief that um that there wasn't a hierarchy of ideas that mapped into the hierarchy of the organization.
In other words, um great ideas could come from anywhere and that we better sort of treat people uh in a much more egatarian sense in terms of where the ideas came from.
And Apple was a very bottoms up company when it came to a lot of its great ideas.
Um, and we hired, you know, truly great people and uh and gave them the room to, you know, to to do great work.

We figured we're paying them all this money, you know, their job is to figure out what to do and tell us.

Um, well, you know, we were very young and um most of the folks were not married and so they could work, you know, 15 hour days.

Right.

Um, I feel it is still my life, but it's not all my life.
Mhm.
It's less, you know, it's less of a percentage, but I I still don't really I've never been able to sort of think of my work and my life as different things.
They're the same thing, but it it it where it used to be, you know, 99% of my life, it's, you know, maybe 50% of my life now.

Um, you know, I I have spent a lot of my my um life in computer graphics.
Uh the Apple 2 was the first personal computer that had color graphics on it.
Uh the Macintosh's ease of use was uh obtained through uh the use of of better graphics than had ever been on a computer to date at that time.
And the Laserwriter was using postscript and was very graphics intensive.
But nothing that I had ever been involved in was as good as what I saw Pixar was doing when I met uh a man named Ed Catmull uh in 1986 and he was then running a division of Lucas Film that was up for sale.
And Ed and I really uh hit it off and he had a dream uh to make the world's first computer animated feature film, which I bought into both uh both spiritually and financially.
And uh so we we formed Pixar in 1986 buying the division from Lucas Film and starting to add people with that vision in mind.
And there's an incredible team of people at Pixar uh that have worked for 10 years to make that dream come true.

You know, I didn't get to animate one frame.
We've got people that are so so great at that that they're the best in the world that uh unfortunately, not being an a visual artist myself, um uh you know, there were several of us that didn't get to to really help make the film per se.
What what I was able to do was was try to make the environment in which, you know, the great team that we have that made the film could successfully make the film.
So I had to negotiate the deal with Disney and all of the other things in terms of running the company uh that were more of the real really just support for the great team that made the film.
The the most incredible thing to me though was it was Pixar was the first time in my life that I went from worrying about, you know, supplying computers to other people to being a consumer of computation.
Um, you know, as an example, each frame in Toy Story took on average 300 megabytes of data to represent all of the elements in that frame.
Wow.
And there's 114,000 frames in that film.
So, you know, each one of those frames took on average three hours to draw using the fastest computers around.
So, we were a consumer of computers for the first time and um it was really great.
You know, when somebody comes out with a faster computer, it used to be, oh no.
And now it's hurray.

# Steve Jobs: The Fresh Air Interview (1996) | Fresh Air

**Source**: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MqSfFcaluHc

**Transcribed**: 2025-12-26 12:09

## Part 1

**[Terry Gross]**: This is Fresh Air. I'm Terry Gross. The history of the computer would have been different if it weren't for my guest, Stephen Jobs. He co-founded Apple Computer, the company that pioneered the user-friendly computer. He oversaw the creation of the Macintosh. He was ousted from the company in 1985 and formed a new computer company called Next. The computer designed by Next was a commercial failure. Now the company is creating software for the worldwide web. Jobs is also the head of Pixar, the computer animation company that produced Toy Story, the first computer animated feature-length film. Jobs became a billionaire when Pixar went public in November. I asked Jobs first about the software Next produces. It's designed to make pages on the worldwide web interactive. I asked him why they're usually static now.

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Well, you know, as you know, the web's a pretty miraculous thing and it was a very simple paradigm that was invented, which was that people could construct uh web pages in some arcane languages, uh one's called HTML. And people could then um touch those pages and view them with a browser. Now, these things are created by human beings for the most part and they they're fairly laborious to create. Once you make one, um people can view it. So you can be viewing a web page along with uh, you know, a quarter million other people looking at exactly the same page. And it's pretty miraculous how it all works and with the internet being wired everywhere and with the navigation that's been put in with the web. Uh you can navigate around the web and look at all of these pages and it's it's it's stunning how how good it is. However, the page you may be looking at is the same page that everyone else is looking at if they happen to be on that website looking at that page. There's nothing custom about it for you. So if you have any questions you want answered, um you're kind of out of luck unless the person that created that page thought to answer your question, you know, a month ago when they created that page. So you might want to say, you know, where is um where's my Federal Express package? And obviously no one created a page to tell you where the Federal Express box you sent yesterday is right now. Um so wouldn't it be great if you could ask questions and those questions could get answered uh via a web page built just for you. And that's why you might want a more dynamic web page in the simplest sense. And Federal Express did just that. They took several months and created some computer programs which when you type in your package tracking number, will go to their main frames, find out all the data about where your package is, get all that data and then, you know, rather than give it to, you know, thousands of gnomes that will create these web pages on the fly, a computer program will build the web page on the fly and send it off to your web browser. And it's it's magic. I mean it was made custom just for you telling you exactly where your package was. And they've got about, you know, 10,000 people a day using the service instead of calling them, which is kind of cool. Now, that's just the tip of the iceberg. It turns out that uh companies when they really want to vend, you know, information about their products or services or they want to start doing commerce on the web, really need to start building these web pages dynamically based on, you know, what the consumer wants. And um that is going to be the next big change in the web.

**[Terry Gross]**: And this is what you're working on, enabling Exactly. these pages to be more interactive.

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Exactly. We call it web objects and uh we announced it about uh three weeks ago. We're giving away the basic version. We put it up on our website and it runs on servers. And we've already uh down I think people have already downloaded uh close to 10,000 copies of it. for free.

**[Terry Gross]**: So, how do you think that um uh the web might change in the near future with the help of the the the type of software that you are producing now?

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Um you know, I think most large companies and medium-sized companies and even small companies are starting to look at the web as the ultimate direct to customer distribution channel. Bypassing all middlemen, going directly from the supplier to the consumer. And that's a pretty powerful concept when you think about it. Uh one of the things that I love is that, you know, a very small company, if they invest a lot in their website, can look just as formidable and just as solid on the web as a very large company can. As a matter of fact, some of the smaller companies are more hip on the web, you know, getting more hip to the web sooner and so they actually look better than some of the large companies do right now. And it's it it's going to be this very leveling phenomenon. Um but I think a tremendous amount of goods and services is going to be sold or at least the demand created for such things over the web.

**[Terry Gross]**: What else do you see in the near future for the web besides the ability to to shop in a more kind of complete uh way through the web?

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Um it's not just shopping for goods and services, it's shopping for information. I mean, you're going to find out already, you know, when I want to find out the movies that are playing around Silicon Valley, I just go up on the local web page and check it out. It's a lot faster than going to the theater going to the uh newspaper. And um a lot faster than calling the theaters, etc. And more and more we're shopping for information on the web. I just recently bought a a Sony, you know, one of the new Sony um camcorders, you know? And I basically I I I went on Sony's web page and I found out all about the ones they offer and picked the one I wanted right from that web page before I even called a store, you know, to to try to find it physically. I basically, you know, the demand to get me to buy that thing was created from Sony's web page. And I think we're going to see more and more of that. You're you're going to be buying information or you're going to finding information and and really making a lot of decisions about what you're going to do with your life or what you're going to purchase from the web.

**[Terry Gross]**: Is the whole idea of going to the store to buy software going to become obsolete too? Do you think we'll be downloading our software from the web?

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Of course. Yeah, there's no question about it. It's a it's just it just there's no question that that will happen and I think it'll happen in the next 24 months. There's some software right now that's still very large. And uh the web on ramps and off ramps to corporations are now very fast, but the the the off ramps to the consumer's homes are still not so fast. And so for buying large software such as CD ROM games and stuff, they'll still be distributed on physical medium media for a while. But when the the uh the off ramps to the consumer get faster, possibly with cable modems in the near future, um then that could could possibly go fully electronic as well.

**[Terry Gross]**: So tell me what else you see for the web beyond the world of retail.

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Yeah, it's not um there's a lot of things happening with the web right now in terms of allowing people access to information that they would just never have before. Uh and what this does is of course, it it lets special interest groups get together. So, you know, you have I I know people who um who have had as an example, a stroke and have gotten on the web and found that there are several uh web pages now devoted to information uh for stroke victims where they can learn about uh, you know, some of the latest treatments, they can learn about avoidance. Uh, you know, the latest in in avoidance uh advice and things like that. And and and those things didn't exist before as well.

**[Terry Gross]**: Steve Jobs is my guest. You started off in the business of designing computers. When did you start thinking that the future wasn't in building the individual computers, but rather in the computer network? I mean because after all what you're doing now is is designing software for the web.

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Right. You know, um I had sort of a landmark visit to Xerox's Park in 1979. That's Palo Alto Research Center where they invented uh a lot of the the cornerstones of the modern graphical user interface. And actually they they showed me what they were doing in 1979 and actually they'd done three things. Uh the first was the the brilliant work they had done on graphical user interfaces. Uh the second was networking. They had over a hundred of their computers at at that time networked in a fully electronic environment using email uh um routinely. And the third thing that they'd done was object-oriented programming. They'd invented small talk and other object-oriented languages as well. And I was so blinded by the the the brilliance of the first, the the graphical user interface, that I didn't even see the other two in 1979. And so when we went to make the Macintosh, um it really completed the job that they had started on the graphical user interface, but really did not address object-oriented technology nor did it address networking.

**[Terry Gross]**: Just to find out terms, the graphic user interface, you're talking about like icons on the computer?

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Uh, yeah, you know, using plain English and menus, icons, drag and drop, all of that stuff. Uh-huh. And and and the objects that you're talking about?

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Object-oriented programming is a technology that is sort of like um it brings to software what the industrial revolution brought to the production of of hard goods, which is reusable parts. Uh the way software is built today is is the same way it was built when it was invented if you will 50 years ago. Everything is custom. And what object-oriented technology lets you do is start to build software with in a much more modern way with reusable components and you end up being able to build software about 10 times faster. And um it's it's slowly starting to seep into the software culture. Uh and I think it's a it you know, it's an unstoppable trend.

**[Terry Gross]**: And this is what you're in the business of now.

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Uh, what Next does is Next works on object-oriented software and has just launched a bunch of web products which incorporate object-oriented software bringing that technology to the web as well.

**[Terry Gross]**: Now, when you started Next, your goal was to make a a new a new kind of computer, but that computer failed on the market. Did that Did that failure help lead you in the direction of working more toward the web, to toward web-oriented software?

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Um you know, when we started Next, uh we I I I guess have to take credit for this. Uh made a a mistake that I've I don't think is terribly uncommon, which is you you you leave something where you were pretty successful and the next thing you do, you try to copy a lot of the paradigms of success that worked the last time. And uh don't realize that the world is changing from underneath your feet. And that's what we did at Next. We made a really great computer. But the world had changed enough to where the door to establish a new uh hardware company really had closed even before we started the company. We just didn't know that at the time. Fortunately, the software that we built for this this computer was so far ahead of its time that even after we exited the hardware business and became a software company, we were still five years ahead of anybody else. And so as Next became a software company, um we really had something that a lot of people wanted.

**[Terry Gross]**: My guest is Stephen Jobs. We'll talk more after a break. This is Fresh Air. Stephen Jobs is my guest, co-founder of Apple Computer, now the chairman of Next Computer Incorporated and also the head of Pixar Studios which made Toy Story. What was the very first computer you had?

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Um, I was very lucky. I I was uh born in San Francisco and I grew up in Silicon Valley. And I uh was able to go to uh NASA Ames Research Center nearby and play with a time sharing computer, which was a, you know, a loud mechanical terminal hooked up with a wire somewhere and there was supposedly a computer on the other end of it. And I got a chance to, you know, program in Fortran and and basic and uh

**[Terry Gross]**: Those are the computer languages of the time.

**[Stephen Jobs]**: The computer languages of the time and I was I was captured by it.

**[Terry Gross]**: And how did you get into the computer business? What made you think I've got this is going to be my life?

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Um, well, I I met uh I met my future partner in Apple, Steve Wozniak when I was about uh oh, I guess about 13 years old and um he was the first person I'd met that knew more about electronics and computers than I did at the time. And we became fast friends and started to build electronic devices together. We built blue boxes together for a while, which were little devices that could allow you to make free phone calls everywhere, illegally, I might add. And

**[Terry Gross]**: Oh, so you were a hacker.

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Yeah. Uh yeah. Yeah. We had we we built the first digital blue box in the whole world. It was wonderful. We had a little our tagline which we put a little card on the bottom of each one was he's got the whole world in his hand. And uh uh the reason we we built a computer uh was that we wanted one and we couldn't afford one. We couldn't afford to buy one. They were thousands of, you know, thousands of dollars at that time. We were just too too teenagers. And uh so we started trying to build them. And uh you know, scrounging parts around Silicon Valley where we could. And after a few attempts, we managed to uh to put together something that was uh the Apple One. And all of our friends uh wanted them too. They wanted to build them. So it turned out that it took um maybe 50 hours to build one of these things by hand. And it was taking up all of our spare time because our friends were not not that skilled at building them. So Waz and I were building them for them. And we thought, you know, if if we could just get what's called a printed circuit board where you could kind of just plug in the parts instead of having to hand wire the whole thing, we could cut the assembly time down from uh you know, maybe 50 hours to to more like, you know, an hour. And so uh Waz sold his HP calculator and I sold my VW microbus and we got enough money together to pay someone to design one of these printed circuit boards for us. And our goal was to just sell them as raw printed circuit boards to our friends and make enough money to recoup our calculator and transportation. And um what happened was that one of the early computers, matter of fact the first computer store in the world, uh which was in Mountain View at the time, said, well, I'll take I'll take 50 of these computers, but I want them fully assembled, which was a twist that we'd never thought of. So we we went and and bought the parts to build 100 computers. And we built 50 of them and delivered them. Um and then we got paid in cash and ran back and paid the people that sold us parts for the parts. And we had then then we had the the classic Marxian profit realization crisis, which was our profit wasn't liquid. It was in 50 computers sitting on the floor. So we decided we had to to start learning about sales and distribution so that we could sell the 50 computers and get back our money. And that's how we got into the business. And we we took we took our idea to to a few companies, one where Waz worked and one where I worked at the time and and uh and neither one was interested in pursuing it, so we we started our own company.

**[Terry Gross]**: Now you you led the team that uh created the Macintosh. And um from what I've read, it sounds like you were really the advocate for having a mouse on the Mac. Why why did you push for that and what was the argument against it?

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Um well, as I mentioned earlier, I went to Xerox Park uh Palo Alto Research Center in 1979 and I saw the early work on graphical user interfaces that they had done. And they had a mouse and uh it was obvious that that you needed a pointing device and a mouse seemed to be the best one. We tried a bunch of other ones subsequently at Apple and a mouse indeed was the best one. We refined it a little bit. Uh we found that, you know, Xerox's had three buttons. We found that people would push the wrong button or be scared that they were going to push the wrong button, so they always looked at the mouse instead of the screen. So we got it down to one button so that you could never push the wrong button and made some refinements like that. Um the Xerox, you know, mouse cost about $1,000 a piece to build. We had to engineer one that cost 20 bucks to build. So we had to do a lot of those kinds of things, but the basic concept of the mouse came originally from uh a company called SRI through Xerox and then to Apple. And there were a lot of people at Apple that just didn't get it. Uh we had we fought tooth and nail with a variety of people there who thought the whole concept of a graphical user interface was crazy, but On what grounds? Uh on the grounds that it either couldn't be done or on the grounds that uh real computer users didn't need, you know, menus in plain English. And real computer users didn't care about, you know, putting nice little pictures on the screen. Um but fortunately, I was the largest stockholder and the chairman of the company, so I won.

**[Terry Gross]**: Steve Jobs is my guest, the co-founder of Apple Computer, now the head of Next Computer Incorporated and also the head of Pixar Studios which made Toy Story. Um do you think that when you were ousted from Apple that people kind of wrote you off? I mean, here you are with these big successes now.

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Oh golly, I don't know. Um I'm sure that a lot of people did and and and that was fine. Uh it it was a very painful time as you might imagine. Um So to be fair, you're the of the company you created.

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Oh, of course. It was a very painful time and um but you know, you just march forward and you try to learn from it. And um one of the things I always I always tried to coach myself on was not being afraid to fail. You know, when you have something that doesn't work out, a lot of times people's reaction is to to get very protective about ever wanting to fall on their face again and and I think that's that that's a big mistake because you never you never achieve what you what you want without falling on your face a few times in the process of getting there. So uh I've tried to not be afraid to fail. And and matter of fact, I've failed quite a bit quite a bit since leaving Apple.

**[Terry Gross]**: Are you surprised at the problems Apple is happen is having now or did you see that coming?

**[Stephen Jobs]**: Um you know, I try not to talk about Apple too much. Uh but what I will say is that that uh you know, the day I left Apple, we had a 10-year lead over Microsoft. Uh and in the technology business, a 10-year lead is really hard to come by. Uh it happens, you know, maybe a company has that once every few decades. Uh whether it be a Xerox or an IBM with main frames. Uh Apple had that with the graphical user interface. And the problem at Apple was that they stopped innovating. You know, if you look at the Mac that ships today, it's 25% different than the day I left and that's not enough for 10 years and and billions of dollars in R&D. And it wasn't that Microsoft was so brilliant or or clever in copying the Mac, it's that the Mac was a sitting duck for 10 years. And that's Apple's problem is that their differentiation evaporated. And uh unlike unlike uh Compact or others who play in the in the Intel Microsoft standard space where they only Compact only has to be 5% better than its competitors for everyone to want to buy their computers. Apple has to be 50 or 100% better uh because when you buy something that is is you know, out of the mainstream a little bit, you take a risk and you want a much bigger reward for taking that risk. And unfortunately that that differentiation has uh not completely evaporated, but uh for the most part it has. And that's the predicament Apple's in now and that's why, you know, cost cutting and other things at Apple are not going to be the cure. The cure for Apple is to innovate its way out of its current predicament. And there's a lot of good people left at Apple that that are capable of doing that with the proper leadership. Which is what's been missing.

**[Terry Gross]**: Some Mac users are afraid that the the Mac operating system is in danger of becoming obsolete in the way that beta video became obsolete because it was it was outdone by uh by VHS. Um what do you think?

**[Stephen Jobs]**: You know, I think with the appropriate leadership at Apple that's not going to happen, but I think, you know, we're going to have to wait and see.

**[Terry Gross]**: Do you care? I mean, how how how how still uh involved, invested do you feel in the future of Apple, the company?
